speaker: fitz
text: In June 2020, the Golden Gate Bridge started to hum.

speaker: fitz
text: In strong winds, people heard it across the city. A deep hum, and a higher whistle. After eighty-three years, why now?

speaker: gauge
text: Did someone tune it? I bet someone tuned it. I brought a tuning fork, just in case.

speaker: fitz
text: Nobody tuned it. But the answer is hiding in the bridge's whole story. Starting with the people who said it couldn't be built.

speaker: gauge
text: I made a list. Gauge's Fix-It List. Every problem this bridge had, I'll fix.

speaker: fitz
text: It's blank.

speaker: gauge
text: It's blank for now.

speaker: fitz
text: Most engineers the city asked thought a bridge here would cost over a hundred million dollars, and couldn't be built at all.

speaker: fitz
text: Many doubted a bridge could survive the brutal wind, tides and fog.

speaker: gauge
text: So who actually wanted it?

speaker: fitz
text: An engineer named Joseph Strauss. He said it could be done for twenty-five to thirty million.

speaker: gauge
text: A hundred million, or thirty million. I like this guy. He's a coupon.

speaker: fitz
text: Plenty of people didn't. The ferry companies would lose business.

speaker: fitz
text: And the War Department, which owned the land on both shores, worried that an enemy could blow up a bridge and block the harbor.

speaker: fitz
text: In 1928, a judge threw out more than two thousand protests against forming the district that would build it.

speaker: fitz
text: Strauss's first design didn't help. The press called it ugly. One critic called it "an upside-down rat trap."

speaker: gauge
text: Fix number one. Build the rat trap.

speaker: fitz
text: It was dropped. Two engineers on the bridge's advisory board, Leon Moisseiff and O. H. Ammann, persuaded Strauss to make it an all-suspension bridge.

speaker: gauge
text: Goodbye, rat trap. You were ugly, but you were mine.

speaker: fitz
text: In 1930, voters approved thirty-five million dollars in bonds. Tolls paid them off.

speaker: fitz
text: And that hundred-million-dollar estimate? It cost thirty-five million in the end.

speaker: gauge
text: Coupon man wins.

speaker: fitz
text: Closer than a hundred million. Still over his coupon.

speaker: gauge
text: Coupon man mostly wins.

speaker: fitz
text: Remember one thing they worried about, though. The wind.

speaker: gauge
text: Clue one.

speaker: gauge
text: So Strauss built it. Whoever's name is on the plaque built it, right?

speaker: fitz
text: Not quite. Strauss was the chief engineer and the driving force. But the mountain of math fell to Charles Ellis, a design engineer on his staff.

speaker: fitz
text: Ellis worked it through with Moisseiff, by telegram.

speaker: fitz
text: Remember Moisseiff. He comes back later.

speaker: fitz
text: According to PBS, Ellis had degrees in mathematics and Greek, but no engineering degree.

speaker: gauge
text: Greek? So the math was all Greek to everyone else.

speaker: fitz
text: In late 1931, Strauss fired him, accusing him of spending too much time and money. The real reasons are still debated.

speaker: fitz
text: When the bridge opened in 1937, Ellis's name was left off its dedication plaque.

speaker: gauge
text: That doesn't seem fair.

speaker: fitz
text: In 2007, the Bridge District said "the record clearly demonstrates that he deserves significant credit for the suspension bridge design." In 2012, a plaque honoring him went up at the bridge.

speaker: fitz
text: The fair version: Strauss pushed it through and ran the job. Moisseiff and Ammann brought the suspension idea. Ellis did the detailed engineering. And an architect, Irving Morrow, shaped how it looks.

speaker: gauge
text: Plaques are not the whole story. Writing that down.

speaker: fitz
text: The north tower stood on a rock ledge near the Marin shore. The south one had to go in open water, more than eleven hundred feet from shore.

speaker: gauge
text: Fix number two. Just drop the tower in the water and let it sink till it hits bottom.

speaker: fitz
text: In fast currents, about a hundred and ten feet down? It needs a dry, solid base first.

speaker: fitz
text: So workers built a long wooden walkway, called a trestle, out to the site. Divers went down into cold water.

speaker: gauge
text: How do you even see down there?

speaker: fitz
text: Barely. It was dark and murky.

speaker: fitz
text: They could only work when the tide turned and the currents eased. That's four times a day.

speaker: fitz
text: Then, in August 1933, in thick fog, a freighter rammed the trestle. That winter, a storm wrecked much of it.

speaker: fitz
text: Crews rebuilt it, then built a huge oval concrete wall around the site, called the fender, to protect the tower from ships in fog, and from the currents.

speaker: fitz
text: Then they pumped about nine point four million gallons of seawater out of it.

speaker: gauge
text: So they built a giant bathtub, and then took all the water out. That's the opposite of a bath.

speaker: fitz
text: That's actually what the bridge district calls it. Inside it, in the dry, they built the base of the south tower.

speaker: fitz
text: Each main cable is just over three feet thick, and nearly a mile and a half long.

speaker: gauge
text: Fix number three. Buy one giant rope. Free shipping.

speaker: fitz
text: You can't lift a cable that big into place. So they built it right where it hangs, one thin wire at a time.

speaker: fitz
text: A spinning wheel ran back and forth along a catwalk, over both towers, laying wire.

speaker: fitz
text: Each cable holds twenty-seven thousand, five hundred and seventy-two wires.

speaker: fitz
text: Both cables together hold eighty thousand miles of wire. That's enough to wrap around the Earth more than three times.

speaker: gauge
text: I've been around the Earth zero times. This wire could do it three times and still have some left.

speaker: fitz
text: The spinning took six months and nine days, and finished months ahead of schedule.

speaker: fitz
text: I'll get this one.

speaker: gauge
text: So the giant rope was a lot of tiny ropes all along.

speaker: fitz
text: For the men high on the steel, Strauss and his resident engineer, Russell Cone, ran a strict safety program for the 1930s.

speaker: fitz
text: Hard hats were required at all times. It was one of the first big projects to require them. And anyone caught drinking or showing off up high was fired on the spot.

speaker: gauge
text: No backflips on the beams. Deleting my backflip plans.

speaker: fitz
text: In 1936, Strauss paid about a hundred and thirty thousand dollars for a huge rope net, hung under the deck from end to end.

speaker: fitz
text: It caught nineteen men. They called themselves the Halfway to Hell Club.

speaker: gauge
text: Nineteen men. That's nineteen people who got to go home.

speaker: fitz
text: But the net couldn't stop everything. Eleven men died building the bridge.

speaker: fitz
text: The first, Kermit Moore, was killed in October 1936, in an accident with falling equipment.

speaker: fitz
text: On February seventeenth, 1937, near the end of the job, a heavy scaffold platform broke away. It fell into the net and tore through it. Ten men died.

speaker: fitz
text: A plaque at the bridge remembers them.

speaker: gauge
text: We'll remember them too.

speaker: fitz
text: Now, that color. The steel arrived already coated in a red lead primer. That's an undercoat, meant to be painted over.

speaker: fitz
text: Irving Morrow, the architect, rode the ferry past the site as the towers went up, saw that reddish primer, and liked it.

speaker: gauge
text: Fix number four. Paint it gray, like a normal bridge.

speaker: fitz
text: Morrow thought that through. The bridge district quotes him: black "would reduce the scale of the bridge more than any other color." Gray would dull it.

speaker: fitz
text: And silver aluminum paint, he warned, would leave the towers "deprived of substance and made tiny."

speaker: gauge
text: Made tiny. Rude. Accurate, but rude.

speaker: fitz
text: The U.S. Navy had its own idea. Black and yellow stripes, so passing ships could see it.

speaker: gauge
text: Stripes. Fix number five. A bumblebee bridge! I love it.

speaker: fitz
text: No.

speaker: gauge
text: It was a very good bumblebee.

speaker: fitz
text: Morrow wanted a warm color, like the hills around it, standing apart from the cool colors of the sky and sea.

speaker: fitz
text: In a 1935 report, quoted by Cabinet magazine, he wrote that the color "is luminous" and is "prominent without insistence."

speaker: gauge
text: Prominent without insistence. That's my new life goal. Starting now. Everyone look at me.

speaker: fitz
text: So the color wasn't really an accident. The primer gave Morrow the idea; the final color came from careful studies.

speaker: fitz
text: Today it's known as International Orange, and the bridge district publishes the recipe, so anyone can mix it.

speaker: gauge
text: International Orange. Clue?

speaker: fitz
text: Hold onto it.

speaker: gauge
text: So do they paint it end to end, and the moment they finish, start all over again?

speaker: fitz
text: That's a popular myth. The district says it's a misconception.

speaker: fitz
text: A permanent crew of a few dozen painters and ironworkers goes after the spots where inspections find rust. Each area gets repainted about every ten to twenty years.

speaker: fitz
text: From the 1960s to 1995, crews stripped the whole bridge and repainted it, replacing the original lead paint.

speaker: gauge
text: Gray, gone. Stripes... gone. For now.

speaker: fitz
text: The bridge is designed to move.

speaker: fitz
text: At the middle of the main span, the deck was designed to swing sideways up to twenty-seven point seven feet.

speaker: gauge
text: Twenty-seven feet?

speaker: fitz
text: That's the design limit. In the 1982 winter storms, it bowed sideways about six to seven feet. In an ordinary steady wind, it's just a few feet.

speaker: fitz
text: It's also designed to move up and down, as much as about sixteen feet in total, as heat stretches the cables, cold shortens them, and traffic weighs the deck down.

speaker: gauge
text: Fix number six. Bolt it down so it can't move.

speaker: fitz
text: Moving is part of the design.

speaker: fitz
text: In 1940, the first Tacoma Narrows Bridge opened in Washington State. Its designer was Leon Moisseiff, who had also worked on the Golden Gate.

speaker: fitz
text: It used the same theory, pushed much further. Where the Golden Gate has steel trusses twenty-five feet deep, Tacoma had a solid steel girder just eight feet deep.

speaker: gauge
text: So Tacoma was skinnier, and solid?

speaker: fitz
text: Yes. That November, in a wind of about forty miles per hour, its deck twisted itself apart.

speaker: gauge
text: Was it the wind pushing at just the right rhythm, like a swing?

speaker: fitz
text: That's how it's often been told. Resonance. But engineers say it was something called flutter.

speaker: fitz
text: Once the deck started twisting, its own motion changed the way the wind flowed around it. So the wind fed the twist, more and more.

speaker: gauge
text: So, not this kind of rhythm.

speaker: fitz
text: Not that kind. Put the fork away for now.

speaker: fitz
text: The Golden Gate got its own warning. On December first, 1951, a storm made its deck twist and bounce enough to close the bridge for a few hours.

speaker: fitz
text: The damage was minor, but engineers recommended stiffening it.

speaker: fitz
text: In 1953 and 1954, crews added a web of diagonal steel bracing across the bottom of the deck, tying the two side trusses together.

speaker: gauge
text: Open box. Twists like a noodle. Closed box. Not budging.

speaker: fitz
text: That's what the bracing did. It turned the deck's open, upside-down U shape into a closed box, which is much harder to twist.

speaker: gauge
text: Fine. You can move, bridge. Just not too much.

speaker: fitz
text: Which brings us back to the hum. The district's wind studies found that a solid railing on the windward side can roll the wind into strong swirls. In extreme winds, that could make the deck unstable.

speaker: fitz
text: Wind-tunnel tests showed the railing needed to be more see-through. The strongest winds there come mainly from the west, so the west railing was replaced with thinner slats that let the wind pass through.

speaker: gauge
text: Final fix. Make the railing solid. No wind gets through, so no hum.

speaker: fitz
text: A solid railing is exactly what they were trying to avoid. That's Tacoma's lesson.

speaker: gauge
text: So the hum comes from the safety upgrade.

speaker: fitz
text: As the wind flows past each slat, tiny swirls of air peel off it. When their rhythm matches the way the slats, or the air between them, naturally vibrate, you get sound.

speaker: fitz
text: It was loud, not dangerous.

speaker: fitz
text: The fix: thin aluminum clips with rubber inserts on the edges of all twelve thousand slats. The district expected to finish fitting them in 2025. And yes, they're painted International Orange.

speaker: gauge
text: Of course they are. Prominent without insistence.

speaker: gauge
text: Did it hum a real note?

speaker: fitz
text: KQED reported the howl at about four hundred and forty hertz. That's the A that musicians tune to. A bridge spokesperson called it a happy coincidence.

speaker: gauge
text: So somebody DID tune it!

speaker: fitz
text: The wind did. By accident.

speaker: fitz
text: So why did the Golden Gate start to sing? Because its new railing was built to let the wind through, a lesson that goes back to 1940.

speaker: gauge
text: Could the clips have little stripes?

speaker: fitz
text: No.

speaker: gauge
text: Then look. Every fix, gone. My list is just thin strips now.

speaker: fitz
text: It's very see-through.

speaker: gauge
text: Lets the wind right through. I'll get some clips.

speaker: fitz
text: If you want to know why bridge roads have gaps in them, we made a Short about that.

speaker: gauge
text: Ooh, what else is built weird? Subscribe and let's find out.
